title: private-network-opaque-tls-interception-sleuth-diary
content:
Summary:

On 2026-12-02 we observed intermittent control-plane API failures for a single customer running Redwood Private in their on-prem VPC. Symptoms were: agent heartbeats accepted from customer hosts but subsequent API calls from those hosts failed TLS handshake or returned short-lived connection resets. The failure pattern was unusual: the TCP sessions established, TLS ClientHello was sent, and then the server (control plane) responded with an unexpected certificate chain (different CA) or no server-side mTLS response, causing the client to drop the connection.

Impact:
- Affected: One customer (prod), ~40% agent heartbeat flapping during windows of 10-20 minutes, causing control-plane metrics to show partial reachability and increased retries.
- Severity: SEV2 (service degraded for customer-managed deployments).
- User visible: occasional failed provisioning and backlog in agent queueing; no data loss observed.

Detection and initial on-call notes (timeline, UTC):
- 2026-12-02 08:03: Alert: increase in control-plane TLS handshake failures from customer A (monitoring alert tls_handshake_fail_rate > 5% over 2m).
- 2026-12-02 08:07: Oncall (Priya) triaged: connectivity to control plane IPs OK (tcp connect), but agent logs show: "SSL handshake failed: peer did not present certificate" and "verify error: self signed certificate in certificate chain".
- 2026-12-02 08:12: Coordinated with SE (Marcus) who reported customer recently rolled out a new perimeter appliance update for outbound inspection.
- 2026-12-02 08:20: Performed controlled replication from customer lab via ssh tunnel — saw same behavior. Began packet captures.
- 2026-12-02 08:40: Confirmed server-side cert chain differed from known Redwood CA in captured packets; observed appliance inserting a forged cert (TLS interception).
- 2026-12-02 09:05: Mitigation applied with customer: create bypass rule for control-plane IPs and port 443 on perimeter appliance. Failures stopped after bypass applied.

Evidence collected:
- tcpdump (abridged):
  08:30:12.123456 IP agent-host.52542 > ctrlplane.rw.io.443: Flags [S], seq 0...
  08:30:12.200112 IP ctrlplane.rw.io.443 > agent-host.52542: Flags [S.], seq 0...
  08:30:12.310549 TLS ClientHello, SNI: control.rw.io
  08:30:12.450001 TLS ServerHello, Certificate: CN=Perimeter-Proxy-Inspection

- openssl s_client run against control plane from customer host (shortened):
  $ openssl s_client -connect control.rw.io:443 -showcerts -servername control.rw.io
  CONNECTED(00000003)
  depth=0 CN = Perimeter-Proxy-Inspection
  verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate
  ---
  No client certificate presented by server (mTLS broken)

- Agent logs (customer host):
  2026-12-02T08:29:35Z ERROR connection: TLS handshake failed: certificate verify failed (self-signed)
  2026-12-02T08:29:36Z WARN heartbeat: retrying, attempt=3

Root cause hypothesis:
- Customer deployed a transparent TLS inspection feature on their perimeter appliance that performs outbound TLS MITM for inspection and replaces the server certificate with a locally-signed cert. For control-plane mutual TLS, the appliance also strips or interferes with client certificate forwarding, so the server does not receive the client cert (or sees altered TLS parameters), causing mTLS handshake failure.
- The appliance was recently updated with a rule that matched all outbound 443 traffic and did not exempt known control-plane IP ranges or ALPN signatures. The transparent proxy is opaque to client/server: connections succeed at TCP level but TLS layer is modified.

Why this was subtle/different from other egress issues:
- Unlike NAT or conntrack exhaustion, TCP sessions were established and long-lived, making network-level checks (ICMP/TCP) appear healthy.
- The proxy altered TLS identity only, so packet-level reachability tools were insufficient; certificate chain inspection was required.

Immediate mitigations taken:
1) Ask customer to add explicit bypass rules for control-plane IP ranges and port 443 on their perimeter appliance (applied 08:55; verified at 09:05).
2) Temporarily allowed agent fallback to plaintext control plane port (if configured) via secure tunnel for this customer while bypass rules propagated (customer-approved exception).
3) Added monitoring alert for TLS cert chain entropy (detect unexpected issuer CN) to escalate faster.

Longer-term fixes and runbook changes (draft):
- Runbook: "detect-and-handle-tls-inspection" (draft steps below). Add to oncall binder and playbooks.
- Pre-deployment checklist for Private installs: require customers to confirm outbound TLS inspection policies and either:
  * Add control-plane IPs to an explicit allowlist for TCP passthrough (recommended), or
  * Configure the appliance to forward mTLS client certificate info (rarely supported), or
  * Use a dedicated non-inspected port/prefix for control-plane (e.g., 8443 + port-based bypass).
- Product change: add a cert-fingerprint verification step in agent bootstrap to detect certificate replacement and surface a clear error message with reason "TLS_INTERCEPTION_DETECTED".
- Telemetry: ship fingerprint hashes of server leaf certificate seen by agents (aggregated, privacy-preserving) to detect divergence from expected CA in <1m windows.
- SE guidance: template firewall rule snippets for common appliances (Palo Alto, Fortinet, Zscaler, Bluecoat) to exempt control plane endpoints. Store in Confluence (linked artifact).

Draft runbook: detect-and-handle-tls-inspection (for oncall)
1) Symptoms: spikes in tls_handshake_fail_rate, logs with "self signed" or "certificate verify failed" and tcp-level connectivity OK.
2) Quick checks:
   - From affected host: curl -v --tlsv1.2 https://control.rw.io/health (observe cert chain in verbose output).
   - From affected host: openssl s_client -connect control.rw.io:443 -servername control.rw.io -showcerts
   - tcpdump -n -s 0 -c 200 tcp port 443 and inspect server Certificate CN (tcpdump -A -s 0 'tcp port 443 and host control.rw.io' then grep for "Certificate:").
3) If intercepted cert present with non-Redwood CA:
   - Ask customer to add bypass for control-plane IPs or port. Provide control-plane IP list and FQDNs (see Confluence link).
   - If bypass cannot be applied quickly: use agent administrative path to rotate to alternate egress (ssh-tunnel overlay) or temporarily enable fallback port if pre-configured.
4) Post-mitigation verification:
   - Verify openssl s_client shows Redwood CA chain.
   - Confirm agent logs show successful mTLS handshake and stable heartbeats for >= 30m.
5) Escalation: If customer cannot modify appliance and vendor does not support passthrough, engage Field Security for secure exception, and Product to schedule a change to use certificate pinning/alternate ports for affected customers.

Notes and follow-ups (owners):
- Marcus: add device-specific allowlist snippets to Confluence and SE playbook (due 2026-12-09).
- Sofia: prototype agent-side certificate-fingerprint telemetry (POC env) and write spec (due 2027-01-15).
- Jamal: add automated alert rule to detect issuer CN divergence and link to runbook (done 2026-12-03).

Appendix (useful commands and snippets):
- tcpdump filter example: sudo tcpdump -n -s 0 -A host control.rw.io and port 443 -c 200 > capture.txt
- openssl check: openssl s_client -connect control.rw.io:443 -servername control.rw.io -showcerts | sed -n '/-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----/,/-----END CERTIFICATE-----/p' | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep Issuer -A1
- sample agent log grep: sudo journalctl -u redwood-agent | grep -E "TLS handshake failed|certificate verify failed|peer did not present certificate"

Short-term customer communication template (for SE):
- Subject: Control-plane connectivity – action required on perimeter inspection appliance
- Body (short): We observed your perimeter device performing TLS inspection that is breaking mutual TLS between Redwood agents and our control plane. Please apply the attached allowlist for control-plane IPs and ports or enable TLS passthrough for control.rw.io. We can assist in validating after changes.

Conclusion:
This incident was caused by transparent TLS interception at the customer perimeter that replaced server certs and interfered with mTLS semantics. It is operationally distinct from conntrack or NAT issues and requires certificate-level detection. The temporary bypass was effective; next steps are to add safer automated detection, documentation for SEs, and product telemetry to surface this class of failure more quickly.
